title: Not just books
subtitle: When a small-town library began lending drills, ukuleles and cake tins, the staff expected a few curious visitors. They got rather more than that.
text: For most of its hundred-year history, the public library in Ashcombe lent books and very little else. By 2019, however, the number of visitors had been falling for a decade, and the town council was openly discussing whether a town of eight thousand people really needed a library at all. {1} Her name was Priya Nair, and she had worked behind the front desk for eleven years.

Nair's idea came from her own garage. Like most of her neighbours, she owned a long list of things she had used only once or twice: a wallpaper steamer, a tent, an electric drill bought to put up a single shelf. {2} If the library could lend those things as easily as it lent novels, she argued, people would have a reason to come back through its doors.

The council was doubtful. Who would pay if a drill came back broken, or did not come back at all? And where, in a building designed for bookshelves, would anyone keep a lawnmower? {3} She asked residents to donate whatever they no longer needed, and she cleared two shelves of out-of-date encyclopaedias to make space for the first items.

The 'Library of Things' opened in March with forty-two objects. Within a week, every one of them was out on loan. The most popular was not the drill, as Nair had predicted, but a set of cake tins shaped like numbers, which were booked for children's birthday parties until the end of the year. {4} One, a guitar, was borrowed by a man who had wanted to learn to play since he was a teenager; a month later he came back for a book of songs.

The fear that things would come back broken has, so far, proved largely unfounded. Borrowers sign a simple form and are asked to report any problems when they return an item. {5} The library now runs a monthly repair café, where volunteers fix anything from toasters to bicycles, and it has become one of the busiest events in the town.

Perhaps the most important change, though, has been in who uses the building. Teenagers come in to borrow speakers and camping stoves; young parents borrow baby carriers and stay for the story hour. {6} Book loans, which had been falling for ten years, rose by a fifth in the first year alone.

Ashcombe's library is no longer on the list of possible closures. It now lends more than four hundred things, including a telescope, a sewing machine and a karaoke set that Nair describes, diplomatically, as 'very well used'. Asked what she would like to add next, she does not hesitate. 'Shelves,' she says. 'We're running out of room.'
sentences: Nair's answer to both questions was to start small and spend nothing.
Many of these new visitors, staff noticed, were leaving with a book as well.
She suspected that, between them, the people of Ashcombe owned hundreds of such objects, most of them sitting forgotten in cupboards.
Not a single item, in fact, has ever come back damaged.
Close behind them came the musical instruments, which the staff had almost decided not to include.
The person who saved it was not a politician or a wealthy donor, but the deputy librarian.
Most do so honestly, and a few retired engineers among them began offering to fix the faults they found.
why: 'It' is the library the council wanted to close; 'the deputy librarian' is then named: 'Her name was Priya Nair'.
'Such objects' are the things used only once or twice; 'hundreds' of them in cupboards become 'those things' the library could lend.
'Both questions' are who would pay and where to keep things; 'spend nothing' and 'start small' explain the donations and the two cleared shelves.
'Them' is the cake tins; 'the musical instruments' are then picked up by 'One, a guitar'.

'Do so' means report problems; the retired engineers lead to the volunteers of the repair café. D is tempting after a paragraph about damage, but 'not a single item' contradicts 'largely unfounded' and leaves the repair café unexplained.
'These new visitors' are the teenagers and young parents; leaving 'with a book as well' explains why book loans 'rose by a fifth'.
